edges.effect_quant: The broad meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials and 2,742 patients found that mobile text messaging improved medication adherence overall (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.52-2.93), while a separate meta-analysis showed that two-way texting outperformed one-way reminders (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.13-1.35 vs no text messaging).
edges.population: adults with chronic disease or long-term prescription treatment
edges.mechanism: Text messaging works by reducing forgetfulness at the exact moment adherence breaks down. When reminders are interactive rather than passive, they also create a small accountability loop that prompts patients to notice missed doses and re-engage with their regimen before nonadherence becomes habitual.
edges.summary: The best anchor is the 16-trial meta-analysis, which found that text messaging meaningfully improves medication adherence across chronic diseases. The nuance is that not all texts work equally well: two-way message systems do better than simple one-way reminders, and some pragmatic hypertension trials suggest that messaging alone is not always strong enough to move downstream clinical outcomes.
edges.caveats: Much of this literature measures adherence over relatively short follow-up and often relies on self-report or refill behavior rather than hard clinical outcomes. The intervention also appears more robust for adherence behavior itself than for blood pressure or other downstream disease markers.
